\chapter{El turno}
\label{ch:es-limpieza}
\hlchaptermodality{453}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read the rota taped up in a stairwell: say whose week it is, say what is and is not included, and check the sheet before changing anything.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la limpieza]{la limpieza — the cleaning}

\label{lesson:ES-C453-limpieza}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{limpio} and \textbf{la mudanza}. One is a description, the other names a job of work. You are about to turn the first into the second.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la limpieza}
\textbf{la limpieza} — cleaning, the cleaning.

\emph{El turno de limpieza} — the cleaning shift. \emph{Productos de limpieza} — cleaning products. \emph{La limpieza del portal es los martes} — the entrance hall is cleaned on Tuesdays.

It names the activity, not the state. For the state you still say \emph{está limpio}. \textbf{Limpiar} is the verb: \emph{hay que limpiar la cocina}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: four endings, four genders settled}]
You now have the full set of Spanish's everyday noun-makers:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ending} & \textbf{example} & \textbf{gender} \\
\midrule
\textbf{-anza} & la mud\textbf{anza} & feminine \\
\textbf{-miento} & el segui\textbf{miento} & masculine \\
\textbf{-eza} & la limpi\textbf{eza} & feminine \\
\textbf{-ción} & la instala\textbf{ción} & feminine \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three of the four are feminine, and \textbf{-miento} is the one to remember as the exception. Learn the ending and the article stops being a guess.

Which ending a given word takes is not predictable — \emph{limpieza} and not \emph{limpiamiento}, \emph{seguimiento} and not \emph{seguianza} — and there is no rule waiting to be found. What is reliable is the gender, and that is most of what you needed.

\textbf{-eza} attaches to adjectives rather than verbs: \emph{limpio} gives \emph{limpieza}, \emph{triste} gives \emph{tristeza}, \emph{pobre} gives \emph{pobreza}. It names the quality, and in this one case also the work of producing it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{limpidus}, clear — as in water you can see through.

English took the same word as \textbf{limpid}, and kept it for water and for prose. Spanish let it drift from \textquotedblleft{}clear\textquotedblright{} to \textquotedblleft{}clean\textquotedblright{}, which is a short walk: a clear stream is a clean one.

There is an older Spanish word for clean, \emph{neto}, from Latin \emph{nitidus}, and it survives in \emph{el peso neto} on a packet. Where Spanish kept two, it usually gave them separate jobs.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the cleaning shift
  \item the kitchen is clean, using the adjective
  \item which of the four endings is masculine
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The cleaning? (\textbf{La limpieza}.) The verb? (\textbf{Limpiar}.) What did \emph{limpidus} mean? (\textbf{Clear} — see-through water.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la instalación]{la instalación — the act, and the thing}

\label{lesson:ES-C453-instalacion}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{arreglar} and \textbf{la oficina}. Somebody put the heating into that building, and there is one word for both halves of that.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la instalación}
\textbf{la instalación} — the installation, the fitting: and also the thing fitted.

\emph{La instalación del aire acondicionado} — putting the air conditioning in. \emph{La instalación eléctrica es vieja} — the wiring is old. And in the plural, the premises: \emph{las instalaciones deportivas} — the sports facilities.

\textbf{Instalar} is the verb, for a boiler and for a program alike.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -ción names the act and then the result}]
This double sense is not a quirk of one word. It is what \textbf{-ción} does:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the act} & \textbf{the result} \\
\midrule
la instalación & fitting it & the wiring \\
la construcción & building it & the building \\
la decoración & decorating & the decor \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The noun names the doing, and then drifts onto whatever the doing left behind. When you meet a \emph{-ción} word, expect both readings and let the sentence pick: \emph{durante la instalación} is the act, \emph{revisar la instalación} is the thing.

Every one is feminine, and every one takes an accent in the singular that it loses in the plural — \emph{instalación}, \emph{instalaciones} — for the reason \emph{almacén} did.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Old French \textbf{installer}: \textbf{in-} plus \textbf{stalle}, a stall — a seat in a choir, from a Germanic word for a standing-place.

To \emph{install} somebody was to put them \textbf{in their stall}: to seat a canon in his place in the cathedral. The word began as ceremony, moved to furniture, and now means putting a boiler on a wall or software on a machine.

The Germanic \emph{stall} is still around in English for a horse's, in \emph{stall} the market stand, and in \textbf{stand} itself. A boiler and a cathedral canon are installed with the same word because both have been put where they belong.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the wiring is old
  \item the sports facilities are closed for cleaning
  \item what \emph{-ción} nouns name besides the act
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The installation? (\textbf{La instalación}.) The plural? (\textbf{Las instalaciones}, accent gone.) What was a \emph{stalle}? (\textbf{A stall} — a standing-place, a seat.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rotativo]{rotativo — it comes round again}

\label{lesson:ES-C453-rotativo}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la rueda} and \textbf{alrededor}. A third word off the same Latin wheel is coming.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: rotativo}
\textbf{rotativo} — rotating, done in turns, on a rota.

\emph{Un turno rotativo} — a rotating shift. \emph{La limpieza es rotativa} — the cleaning goes round the neighbours. \emph{Presidencia rotativa} — a chairmanship that passes from one member to the next.

The idea is always the same: the job does not stay with one person, it comes round. \textbf{Rotar} is the verb, and \textbf{la rotación} the noun with the ending from the lesson before this one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -ivo describes what a thing does}]
\textbf{-ivo} makes an adjective meaning \textquotedblleft{}of the kind that does this\textquotedblright{}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{adjective} \\
\midrule
rotar & rotat\textbf{ivo} — that rotates \\
informar & informat\textbf{ivo} — that informs \\
decorar & decorat\textbf{ivo} — that decorates \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

It is not about being in the act. A \emph{turno rotativo} is not rotating at this moment; it is a shift \textbf{of the rotating kind}. The ending names a habit or a capacity, which is why \emph{un cartel informativo} is informative whether or not anybody is reading it.

English has the identical ending in \emph{rotative}, \emph{informative}, \emph{decorative}, and uses it the same way.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{rota}, wheel — for the third time, and it is worth stopping on.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{how the wheel got in} \\
\midrule
\textbf{la rueda} & straight down from \emph{rota}, vowel broken by stress \\
\textbf{alrededor} & \emph{retrō} bent sideways by \emph{rota} \\
\textbf{rotativo} & lifted from \emph{rota} whole, by scholars \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three words, three routes out of one Latin noun. \emph{Rueda} is what centuries of speakers did to it. \emph{Rotativo} is what a writer did to it in one step, keeping the \textbf{o} intact because it never passed through anybody's mouth on the way.

That difference — worn down by speech, or lifted whole from a book — is the single most useful thing to notice about Spanish vocabulary, and here you can see both outcomes of it side by side.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a rotating shift
  \item the cleaning goes round the neighbours
  \item why \emph{rueda} has \emph{ue} and \emph{rotativo} does not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Rotating? (\textbf{Rotativo}.) The verb? (\textbf{Rotar}.) What does \emph{-ivo} name — an action happening, or a habit? (\textbf{A habit or a capacity}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[consultar]{consultar — look it up}

\label{lesson:ES-C453-consultar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{revisar} and \textbf{el documento}. Both are about paper, and what you do to it differs.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: consultar}
\textbf{consultar} — to look up, to check, to consult.

\emph{Consulte el horario} — check the timetable. \emph{Lo consulto y te digo} — I'll look into it and get back to you. \emph{Consultar con el jefe} — to check with the boss.

Two nouns come with it: \textbf{la consulta}, which is both the query and a doctor's surgery, and \textbf{el consultorio}, the consulting room.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: consultar, revisar, mirar}]
Three verbs that all come out as \textquotedblleft{}check\textquotedblright{} in English, now separated by what you are after:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you want} & \textbf{the verb} \\
\midrule
a fact you do not have & \textbf{consultar} \\
faults in something you do have & \textbf{revisar} \\
to aim your eyes at it & \textbf{mirar} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Consulto el horario} — I do not know the time and the timetable does. \emph{Reviso el horario} — I am checking the timetable for mistakes, which is a different errand entirely. \emph{Miro el horario} — my eyes are on it, and the sentence has said nothing about why.

Note the preposition: you \emph{consultar} a document directly, but \emph{consultar \textbf{con}} a person. The \textbf{con} marks that the other party can answer back.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{consultare}, the repeated form of \textbf{consulere} — to take counsel, to deliberate.

The Roman \textbf{consul} is the same root: the officer who takes counsel for the state. And \textbf{el consejo} — advice, and a council — came down the spoken road from \emph{consilium}, a close relation.

So \emph{consultar} and \emph{el consejo} are family, and the pair shows the split this chapter keeps meeting: \emph{consejo} is worn smooth by centuries of speech, \emph{consultar} was lifted from Latin by clerks with the \textbf{l} and the \textbf{t} still in place.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item check the timetable
  \item I'll check with the boss and tell you
  \item which preposition goes before a person
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To look up? (\textbf{Consultar}.) To check for faults? (\textbf{Revisar}.) Which Roman officer shares the root? (\textbf{The consul} — one who takes counsel.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(la limpieza, la instalación …]{(la limpieza, la instalación, rotativo, consultar) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R453-repaso-limpieza}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all four: \emph{the cleaning}, \emph{the installation}, \emph{rotating}, \emph{to look up}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same Latin word, twice, differently}]
Two pairs in this chapter show the single most useful fact about Spanish vocabulary: a Latin word can arrive \textbf{twice}, once through speech and once through books, and the two arrivals look nothing alike.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{worn down by speech} & \textbf{lifted from the page} \\
\midrule
la r\textbf{ue}da & r\textbf{o}tativo \\
el cons\textbf{ejo} & cons\textbf{ultar} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The left-hand column went through hundreds of years of mouths: vowels broke, consonants softened, syllables fell out. The right-hand column was copied out by a clerk who could read Latin, so it kept its shape.

The practical payoff: when a Spanish word looks \textbf{more} like its Latin or English cousin, it is usually the later, bookish arrival — and it will belong to writing, forms and notices rather than to the kitchen. That is a register clue you can read straight off the spelling.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the four noun-makers, complete}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ending} & \textbf{example} & \textbf{gender} \\
\midrule
-anza & la mudanza & feminine \\
-miento & el seguimiento & masculine \\
-eza & la limpieza & feminine \\
-ción & la instalación & feminine \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three feminine, one masculine. Which ending a word takes has to be met word by word; the gender never does.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the cleaning shift is on a rota
  \item check the timetable and tell me
  \item which of \emph{rueda} and \emph{rotativo} came through speech
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
All four again, in Spanish, without looking. Then one sentence putting somebody on a cleaning rota.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(el cuadro de turnos) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C453-sintesis-limpieza}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la limpieza} and \textbf{rotativo}. The notice below puts them in the same line.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
A sheet taped inside the entrance hall. Read it, then answer.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{TURNOS DE LIMPIEZA — ESCALERA B}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
La \textbf{limpieza} del portal es \textbf{rotativa}, una semana por vivienda.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Esta semana: 3º izquierda. La próxima: 3º derecha.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
No se limpia la \textbf{instalación} de la caldera. De eso se encarga la empresa.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Para cambiar de semana, \textbf{consulten} el cuadro antes de escribir en él.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item whose turn it is this week and whose it is next
  \item the one thing the neighbours do not have to clean
  \item what you must do before changing your week
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{La instalación de la caldera} is the noun in its second sense — not the act of fitting the boiler, which happened years ago, but the pipes and tank it left behind. Nothing in the sentence announces which reading is meant; \emph{no se limpia} settles it, because you cannot clean an act.

\textbf{Rotativa} agrees with \emph{la limpieza}, and it is doing the work of a whole English clause: \textquotedblleft{}goes round the flats in turn\textquotedblright{}. One adjective, because Spanish had a word for the wheel and built on it.

Then \textbf{consulten}: \emph{ustedes}, plural and formal, the register of a notice addressed to every household at once. And \emph{se encarga}, once again the \emph{se} that lets a sentence say what happens without naming who.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four lines for a stairwell notice: say the cleaning is on a rota, say whose week it is, say the boiler installation is not included, and tell people to check the sheet first.

Then check yourself: did \emph{rotativa} agree with \emph{la limpieza}, and did you use the \emph{ustedes} command?
\end{tcolorbox}
